hookLine: The ticket was written. Then they made him wait for a dog.

captions.text: How long can the police keep
you at the side of the road?
Not why they can stop you —
how long they can hold you once they have. Just after midnight on a dark Nebraska
highway, a driver drifts onto the shoulder
for a second, and a patrol car
lights up behind him.
The officer checks his papers, writes a warning, hands everything back. The stop is over;
its business is done.
And then nothing moves. No one tells the driver he is free to go. He waits.
Seven minutes.
Eight.
A second cruiser rolls up,
a dog begins to circle the car
and the whole night turns
on a question the Supreme Court would
take up three years later:
not whether the stop was legal,
but whether it lasted too long.
We spend a lot of energy arguing
about when the police can pull you over.
This case is about something quieter,
and more personal —
the clock.
Once an officer has a reason
to stop you, how many minutes does
that reason buy?
Can they finish the ticket,
then keep you sitting there on a hunch while they go looking
for something else?
In 2015, in a case called Rodriguez
v.
United States, the Supreme Court drew
a line —
not in space, but in time.
Over the next twelve minutes:
a traffic stop that ran a few
minutes too long, the weight the Court
hung on a single word,
"mission," and why those seven or eight
minutes still shape every stop on every
road today.
Just after midnight on March 27,
2012, Dennys Rodriguez was driving a Mercury
Mountaineer down a Nebraska highway
when it drifted onto the shoulder for a moment, then swung back.
That was enough.
Under Nebraska law, driving on the shoulder
is a violation, and an officer named
Morgan Struble was watching.
Struble was no ordinary patrolman.
He was a K-9 officer,
and riding in the back
of his car was a trained drug-detection
dog.
What happened next was,
for a while, completely routine.
Struble pulled Rodriguez over,
walked up to the window, and did the ordinary things.
He collected the license,
the registration, the proof of insurance.
He ran his checks.
He asked the usual questions.
Then he did the thing that, on paper, ends a traffic stop: he wrote Rodriguez a warning,
not even a ticket,
just a written warning,
explained it, and handed the documents back
Stop and notice what that moment means.
The reason for the stop was that the car had touched the shoulder, and Struble had now dealt
with it.
The warning was written.
The papers were returned.
In the language the Court would later use, the "mission" of the stop
was complete.
By any ordinary understanding, Rodriguez was now free to drive away.
He wasn't.
Struble never said, "You're free to go."
Instead he asked for something more —
permission to walk his dog around
the car.
Rodriguez said no.
And that refusal did not end
the encounter.
It started the clock this whole case is about.
Because Rodriguez would not consent,
Struble ordered him to shut off the engine, step out,
and wait by the road.
He radioed for a second officer.
And for the next seven to eight
minutes, Rodriguez stood on the shoulder
of a dark highway,
no longer being ticketed,
no longer processed for anything at all,
simply held.
When the backup finally arrived,
Struble retrieved his dog and led it around the Mountaineer. On the second pass,
the dog alerted, and a search turned
up methamphetamine.
From the first flash of the patrol lights to that alert,
about twenty-nine minutes had passed,
and what the search found came
in the stretch of time after the warning, not before.
So here is the hard problem.
Everything Struble did up to the warning was clearly legal.
Stopping a car that drifts onto
the shoulder —
legal.
Checking a license — legal. A dog sniff, on its own, the Court had said in an earlier
case, is not even a "search".
Each piece, by itself,
was fine.
What turned this into a constitutional case
was the order they came in,
and the gap in the middle:
the officer finished the traffic stop,
then kept the driver there,
with no ticket left to write, waiting for a dog. The government's answer was, in essence:
what's the harm?
It was only seven or eight minutes.
Officers, it argued, should have a little breathing room, a small buffer to run
a dog around a car,
especially with a second unit
on the way for safety.
A few extra minutes is such
a small thing, the government said,
that the Constitution shouldn't even count
it.
In legal terms, it was "de minimis"
too slight to notice.
And that argument has real force.
Seven minutes is not long.
If you have ever idled at a red light or in a drive-through,
you have surrendered more without a second thought.
Why should a brief,
careful delay, done partly for the officer's
own safety, suddenly count as a violation
of your rights?
On April 21, 2015,
the Supreme Court gave its answer —
six votes to three.
Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg wrote
for the majority, and her reasoning turned
on that one word:
mission.
A traffic stop, she wrote,
is a seizure —
for those minutes, the government is holding you —
and it is justified only by its purpose. The stop exists to handle the violation
and the safety concerns that ride along
with it:
checking your license, your registration,
your insurance, whether there are warrants out for you.
Those tasks are the mission.
And the authority to hold you,
the Court said, ends when the tasks
tied to the traffic violation are —
or reasonably should have been —
completed.
A stop may last as long
as its job takes,
and no longer.
A dog sniff is not part
of that job.
Sniffing for drugs, the Court noted,
has nothing to do with keeping a car safe on the road;
it is a different errand entirely —
ordinary crime detection, aimed at finding evidence.
So when Struble held Rodriguez past
the warning to run the dog,
he was no longer doing traffic-stop work.
He was doing something else, on the government's initiative, with the driver's time.
Then the Court did the thing that makes the case famous. It refused to let the outcome hang
on the order the officer happened
to choose.
It would not matter,
Ginsburg wrote, whether the sniff came before
the warning or after it.
One thing mattered:
did holding the driver for the dog
add time to the stop?
An officer cannot bank the minutes he saves by working fast
and then spend them on an unrelated
investigation.
A stop, she wrote —
quoting an earlier case —
becomes unlawful when it is "prolonged beyond the time reasonably required to complete
the mission."
And that is why the government's
"it was only a few minutes" argument lost.
The Court refused to measure the intrusion by whether it felt big or small.
The question was not how long
the extra delay ran,
but whether the officer had any authority
to impose it at all.
Once the mission was finished,
he did not.
Seven minutes past the end
of a stop is still seven minutes
the government had no reason to hold
you.
It is worth being precise about what the Court did not do. It did not ban dog sniffs.
It did not ban traffic stops,
or order officers to rush,
or say the police can never act
on a hunch.
And it did not set Rodriguez free
In fact, it left a second door wide open. If Struble had a real,
specific reason to suspect Rodriguez of something
beyond the traffic violation —
genuine reasonable suspicion —
then holding him for the dog might have been perfectly lawful.
So the Court sent the case back to the lower courts to answer exactly that:
setting the timing rule aside,
did the officer have independent grounds
to keep Rodriguez waiting?
The dissenters thought the answer was plainly yes.
Justice Clarence Thomas, joined by Justice Samuel Alito, argued that the whole encounter
all twenty-nine minutes —
was reasonable, and that the officer had
enough to justify the wait regardless.
Alito added that the majority's rule
was strangely formal:
an officer who paused to call
for backup before running the dog —
a sensible safety step —
would now be penalized for the timing
Their point was not that time doesn't
matter.
It was that a short,
careful delay by a lone officer
at midnight was reasonable —
which is the very thing the Fourth Amendment asks.
But the majority's line held,
and its strength
is that it is clean.
It does not ask a judge
to guess whether a delay felt long
or short, or whether a hunch
was strong enough to be worth a few minutes.
It asks a simpler question:
is the traffic stop still doing traffic-stop
work?
The moment the mission is finished, the clock stops, and holding you any
longer needs its own reason.
That rule now sits behind millions
of ordinary stops.
Every time an officer finishes a ticket
and then lingers —
one more question, one more check,
a slow walk around the car —
Rodriguez is the case that asks
the quiet question underneath:
is the mission over?
Because if it is,
the time that comes after belongs
to you.
So go back to that dark shoulder
in Nebraska, just after midnight.
The warning was written.
The papers were handed back.
The reason for the whole encounter was finished —
and still the driver could not leave
The Supreme Court looked at those seven
or eight silent minutes and said
they were not the government's to take.
Your rights, it turns out,
are not only about where the state can go.
They are about how long it can
keep you.
And that is the thread running quietly
through all of this.
Three times now, we have watched
the law draw its line
in a different place.
Around the home, and the walls
that hold your heat inside.
Around the person, and words spoken
where no wall stands at all.
And now around time itself —
the minutes at the side
of a road that no one
is entitled to take from you.
The same idea keeps surfacing
in a new disguise:
your freedom lives at the edges,
in exactly the places the state would
find it easiest to slip past.
We call the Fourth Amendment a wall
around your private life.
But it may be truer to call
it a line —
drawn sometimes in space, sometimes in sound, and here,
in time.
Wherever it runs, the task
is the same:
to mark the point where the government
has to stop, and you begin.
That is where your rights have always lived. Right at the edge.
